items.title: Goal "parse metadata at the edge": which check fits
items.body:
Audit rows store `metadata` as a JSON string, and `AuditLogDto` types it as `metadata: string`, so the API returns it as a quoted string the client must parse again. Audit exercise 4 parses it once in the service (with a fallback for bad JSON) and changes the DTO type to an object.

The matching Check observes exactly that: the response shows `"metadata": { "lineCount": 1 }`, an object, not a quoted string, and `npm run typecheck` passes, proving the shared DTO type was updated to match.

Why the other Checks do not fit:
- the user-buyer dashboard Check belongs to audit exercise 3, "Decouple the admin panel".
- the newest-rows Check (reconciliation_completed and order.reserved) belongs to audit exercise 1, "Read the trail"; it reads metadata but does not care whether it is a string.
- the entityType/entityId and limit=500 Check belongs to audit exercise 2, "Add filters".

items.title: Goal "see the role ranking": which check fits
items.body:
Design exercise 2 asks you to act as `user-buyer` and call two endpoints: reserve and the CSV export. The point is to *see* that roles are ranked. Reserving needs warehouse manager or higher; the export is allowed from rank 1 up, which includes buyers.

The matching Check shows both outcomes. Reserve returns 403 listing `requiredRoles: ["warehouse_manager", "admin"]`, and the export returns 200. One call refused, one allowed, for the same user: that is the ranking made visible.

Why the other Checks do not fit:
- the reserve-response Check (status allocated, west green pack reserved 38) belongs to design exercise 1, "Reserve an order end to end"; it is run as the warehouse lead, who is allowed.
- the four-alerts, three-notifications Check belongs to design exercise 4, "Make reconciliation warehouse-aware".
- the order.reserved row with actorId user-warehouse-lead Check belongs to design exercise 3, "Pass the actor through".

const roleRank: Record<string, number> = { viewer: 0, buyer: 1, warehouse_associate: 1, warehouse_manager: 2, admin: 3, }

items.title: Why a warehouse associate can download the CSV export
items.body:
`requireRole` does not check whether your role is *in* the list. It turns the list into a minimum rank: `Math.min(...allowedRoles.map((role) => roleRank[role] ?? 99))`. The ranks are buyer 1, warehouse_manager 2, admin 3, so the minimum is 1. Then it lets through anyone whose rank is at least 1. `warehouse_associate` also has rank 1, so it passes, though it is not named in the list. The design doc: "Roles are ranked, not listed."

Why the others are wrong:
- Being named in the list is not what is checked; the rank is.
- No separate buyer membership is needed; rank 1 is enough.
- `warehouse_associate` has rank 1, not 0 (viewer is 0).

items.title: Why an unknown x-user-id gets a 500
items.body:
`authenticateRequest` looks up the user named in `x-user-id`. For "nobody" no user is found, so it calls `next(new Error('Authenticated user was not found.'))`. That is a plain `Error`, with no HTTP status attached. The app's error handler only treats a `ZodError` (bad input) specially; "everything that is not a `ZodError`" becomes a 500. So a request with an unknown identity gets a server error instead of 401. The design doc lists it as "Unknown users cause a 500."

Why the others are wrong:
- The request never reaches `requireRole`, so no rank and no 403.
- 401 would be the right answer, but nothing maps this error to 401.
- Only a *missing* header falls back to the system user; a wrong id fails.

excerpts.quote: if (!actor) { next(new Error('Authenticated user was not found.')) return }
- **Unknown users cause a 500.** `authenticateRequest` passes a plain `Error` to `next` (`auth.ts:24`), and the error handler maps everything that is not a `ZodError` to 500 (`app.ts:111-119`).

items.title: Goal "harden the CSV": which check fits
items.body:
Today `csvCell` only quotes values with a comma or a double quote. Design exercise 5 adds two protections: quote values containing a line break (so one value cannot break into two rows), and put a single quote in front of values starting with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` (so a spreadsheet shows them as text instead of running them as formulas).

The matching Check tests exactly those two rules in a unit test: `csvCell('=SUM(A1)')` returns `'=SUM(A1)`, and a value containing a newline comes back wrapped in double quotes.

Why the other Checks do not fit:
- the four-alerts, three-notifications Check belongs to design exercise 4, "Make reconciliation warehouse-aware".
- the order.reserved row with actorId user-warehouse-lead Check belongs to design exercise 3, "Pass the actor through".
- the 403-with-requiredRoles Check belongs to design exercise 2, "See the role ranking".
None of them looks at a CSV cell.

excerpts.quote: *Goal:* quote values containing a line break, and prefix values starting with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` with a single quote. *Check:* a unit test shows `csvCell('=SUM(A1)')` returns `'=SUM(A1)` and a value containing a newline comes back wrapped in double quotes.
function csvCell(value: string | number) { const text = String(value) return text.includes(',') || text.includes('"') ? `"${text.replaceAll('"', '""')}"` : text }

items.title: Concept: matching a Goal with the Check that proves it
items.body:
Two docs end with numbered exercises, each with a **Goal** (what to do or build) and a **Check** (something you can observe that proves it worked). final-system-design.md has five: reserve an order end to end, see the role ranking, pass the actor through, make reconciliation warehouse-aware, and harden the CSV. 002-audit-log-viewer.md has four: read the trail, add filters, decouple the admin panel, and parse metadata at the edge.

Several goal-check quizzes give one Goal and four Checks drawn from the same list. To match them:

- Read the Goal and name the code it changes or the request it makes.
- For each Check, ask what it observes: an HTTP response, a database count, a field in the audit log, a unit test.
- The right Check observes exactly what the Goal changes, and would look different if the Goal were not done.

Checks that mention an earlier exercise ("after exercise 1") depend on it, which is another clue to which exercise they belong to.

excerpts.quote: Each has a **Goal** and a **Check** you can observe.

items.title: Reservations are written active for 72 hours
items.body:
**Key: status active, with expiresAt 72 hours after the row is written.**

For every line with a balance, the service increments `reserved` and then calls `tx.stockReservation.create` with `status: 'active'` and `expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 72 * 60 * 60 * 1000)`. The order itself moves to `allocated`, but that is the order's status, not the reservation's. The design document adds that nothing reads `expiresAt` yet.

Why the others are wrong:
- *pending, no expiry*: both fields are set at creation.
- *promisedShipBy*: the expiry is computed from the current time.
- *allocated, 24 hours*: allocated is the order status, and the window is 72 hours.

excerpts.quote: status: 'active', expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 72 * 60 * 60 * 1000),

items.title: Start here: Atlas Fulfillment and its architecture docs
items.body:
Atlas Fulfillment is a TypeScript warehouse and inventory app built as a modular monolith: an Express API with Prisma, a React operations console, shared domain rules and a worker. The current build is small: one tenant, two warehouses, a dashboard, and two operations that change data (reserve a sales order, run low-stock reconciliation).

Read in this order:

- **README.md**: what the app is and the commands to set it up.
- **docs/architecture/final-system-design.md**: the repo structure, the major workflows step by step with line anchors, the section "What this design looks like under review", and five Goal/Check exercises.
- **docs/architecture/architecture-journal.md**: how the design got here, and the open decisions.
- **docs/features/002-audit-log-viewer.md**: one feature as built, with four more exercises.
- **docs/features/000-backlog.md**: what comes next and where each item starts in the code.

The concept quizzes follow the "Major Workflows" and "under review" sections. Open each anchor (for example `orders.service.ts:46-48`) and read the lines.

excerpts.quote: It is built as a modular monolith for learning how realistic business software grows: domain rules, database schema, API modules, background jobs, frontend workflows, tests, and architecture documentation.

- `docs/architecture` contains architecture planning, journal entries, and system design notes. - `docs/features` contains feature plans and build journals. - `docs/walkthroughs` explains important files for learning. - `prisma` contains the schema, local SQLite initializer, and seed data. - `src/shared` contains domain rules and API contracts. - `src/server` contains Express app composition and backend modules. - `src/client` contains frontend API functions and fallback data. - `src/worker` contains background job entrypoints. - `tests` contains domain and API tests.

items.title: Only the order's warehouse counts
items.body:
**Key: a failure with available 0, because no balance exists in that warehouse.**

`reserveSalesOrder` loads balances with `where: { warehouseId: order.warehouseId, skuId: { in: ... } }`, so other warehouses never reach `planReservation`. There, `balances.find(...)` returns nothing for the line, `available` is 0, and the `!balance` branch returns a failure with the reason 'No inventory balance exists for this SKU in the selected warehouse.'

Why the others are wrong:
- *the other warehouse covers it*: reservations are per warehouse, and other warehouses are not loaded.
- *the other warehouse's count*: `available` is set to 0 when the balance is missing.
- *skipped*: the missing-balance case is reported as a failure, not dropped.

items.title: Who the API thinks you are with no x-user-id header
items.body:
`authenticateRequest` reads the caller's id with `request.header('x-user-id') ?? systemUserId`. If the header is missing, `??` falls back to `systemUserId`, the system user. That user is the most privileged one. So an anonymous request is treated as the admin. The design doc lists it plainly: "Missing header means admin." It adds that any `x-user-id` value is trusted as-is, so there is no real authentication here.

Why the others are wrong:
- The fallback is the system user, not a low-privilege viewer.
- Nothing remembers previous users.
- There is no 401 for a missing header; the code substitutes the system user.

excerpts.quote: const requestedUserId = request.header('x-user-id') ?? systemUserId const actor = await prisma.user.findFirst({ where: { id: requestedUserId, tenantId: defaultTenantId }, })
- **Missing header means admin.** `authenticateRequest` falls back to `systemUserId` (`auth.ts:18`), so an anonymous request is the most privileged user. Any `x-user-id` value is trusted as-is.

items.title: At the reorder point already counts as low
items.body:
**Key: low, because the 8 units available sit right at the reorder point.**

`availableToPromise` gives `Math.max(0, 100 - 92)`, which is 8. `stockHealth` returns `stockout` only when that is 0 or less. Next it asks `isLowStock`, which is true when `available <= reorderPoint` **or** `onHand <= safetyStock`. The first test is `8 <= 8`, so the balance is `low`.

Why the others are wrong:
- *healthy, onHand is high*: either test is enough; the reorder-point test already fired.
- *stockout*: 8 units are still available.
- *strictly below*: the comparison is `<=`.

excerpts.quote: return availableToPromise(balance) <= balance.reorderPoint || balance.onHand <= balance.safetyStock

items.title: What the console shows when the API is down
items.body:
In `App.tsx`, `refresh` loads the dashboard and the audit logs inside a `try`. If either request fails, the `catch` runs `setDashboard(fallbackDashboard)`: it replaces all the data with built-in sample data from `src/client/fallbackData.ts`. It also sets a status message ending "Showing local fallback data." So every table fills with realistic sample rows. The design doc warns: "The status line says so, but every table then shows sample data that looks real." An operator could easily mistake it for live inventory.

Why the others are wrong:
- The tables are not empty; they are filled with sample data.
- Nothing is cached in localStorage; the fallback is a fixed file in the code.
- There is no error page; the dashboard renders with the fallback.

items.title: Why an atomic increment can still over-reserve on PostgreSQL
items.body:
The service first *reads* the balances (`findMany`) and decides with `planReservation`. Only later does it run `reserved: { increment: line.quantity }`. The increment itself is atomic, but the decision to do it was based on the earlier read. This is a **check-then-act** race. Two reservations for different orders can both read "40 available", both decide "yes", and both increment, together reserving more than exists. On SQLite, its single-writer locking limits this. On PostgreSQL at its default isolation level, it can happen. The fix: tie the check to the write, with a conditional update (`WHERE onHand - reserved >= :qty`) or row locking.

Why the others are wrong:
- The doc's race has nothing to do with expiry timing.
- A transaction alone does not serialise this at PostgreSQL's default isolation level.
- The doc says the increment *is* atomic; the gap is between read and write.

excerpts.quote: const balances = await tx.inventoryItem.findMany({ where: { warehouseId: order.warehouseId, skuId: { in: order.lines.map((line) => line.skuId) }, }, }) const decision = planReservation(order.lines, balances)
await tx.inventoryItem.update({ where: { id: balance.id }, data: { reserved: { increment: line.quantity } }, })
The increment itself is atomic, but the decision is based on the earlier read.

items.title: What is saved when planReservation reports a shortage
items.body:
When `planReservation` says there is not enough stock, `decision.ok` is false and the service takes the failure branch. It writes one audit row with `action: 'order.reservation_failed'` for the order, and returns the failures. It does *not* throw. Because nothing throws, the transaction commits normally, so that audit row is saved, while no balances, reservation rows or order status are changed. The design doc: "The transaction still commits, so the failed attempt is recorded." A shortage is treated as a normal business outcome, not as a crash.

Why the others are wrong:
- No partial reservations are made; the failure branch runs before any increment.
- It does not roll back; nothing throws, so the audit row is committed.
- The order's status is not changed, and an audit row *is* written.

excerpts.quote: if (!decision.ok) { await tx.auditLog.create({ data: { id: `audit-reservation-failed-${Date.now()}`, tenantId: defaultTenantId, actorId: systemUserId, action: 'order.reservation_failed',
4. On failure, write an `order.reservation_failed` audit row and return the failures (`:58-72`). The transaction still commits, so the failed attempt is recorded.

items.title: Goal "warehouse-aware reconciliation": which check fits
items.body:
Today reconciliation skips a SKU if an unread notification with the title "Low stock: " plus the SKU code exists. The title has no warehouse in it, so a SKU low in two warehouses only gets one notification. - the order.reserved row with actorId user-warehouse-lead Check belongs to design exercise 3, "Pass the actor through".
- the reserve-response Check (status allocated, west green pack reserved 38) belongs to design exercise 1, "Reserve an order end to end".

Design exercise 1 sets up a fresh database, starts the API and reserves order `so-10035` as the warehouse lead with `curl`. A full end-to-end Check must show three things: the API answered, the database changed correctly, and repeating the request is safe.

items.title: Concept: how an order reservation moves through the code
items.body:
The most important workflow is **reserving a sales order**: setting aside stock in a warehouse for an order's lines. The design document says the endpoint loads the order and the warehouse's balances, plans the reservation, updates reserved quantities, creates reservation rows, updates the order's status and writes an audit log, all in one transaction.

Some vocabulary you need for every reservation quiz:

- **onHand**: units physically in the warehouse.
- **reserved**: units already promised to orders.
- **available** (available-to-promise): roughly `onHand - reserved`, never below zero.
- **planReservation** (in `src/shared/inventoryRules.ts`): a pure function that decides, from the lines and balances, whether the reservation can go ahead. It does not touch the database.

The service in `orders.service.ts` calls it inside a Prisma transaction and then writes the results. When a quiz asks "what is saved?", separate the *decision* (pure, in shared rules) from the *writes* (in the service), and read the branch the decision leads to.

excerpts.quote: Inventory availability is calculated as `onHand - reserved`, clamped at zero (`src/shared/inventoryRules.ts:25-27`).
The reservation endpoint loads the order and warehouse balances, plans the reservation, updates reserved quantities, creates stock reservation rows, updates order status, writes an audit log

items.title: Why ids built from Date.now() can collide
items.body:
`Date.now()` returns the current time in milliseconds. A computer can easily do two things within the same millisecond. If two failed reservations are written in the same millisecond, both audit rows get the id `audit-reservation-failed-` followed by the same number. The id is the table's primary key, which must be unique, so the second insert fails. The design doc lists this under "Time-based IDs": audit, event, outbox, reservation and notification ids all embed `Date.now()`. A random id or one generated by the database avoids it.

Why the others are wrong:
- `Date.now()` is a UTC millisecond count; it carries no timezone offset.
- It is not unique: many calls in one millisecond return the same value.
- The doc's concern is collisions, not a year-2038 limit (JavaScript times do not overflow then).

excerpts.quote: id: `audit-reservation-failed-${Date.now()}`,

- **Time-based IDs.** Audit, event, outbox, reservation and notification IDs embed `Date.now()` (for example `orders.service.ts:61`, `:87`, `:104`, `:114`, `:123`). Two writes of the same kind in the same millisecond produce the same primary key, and the second insert fails.

items.title: Why two 30-unit lines for one SKU both pass with 40 available
items.body:
`planReservation` uses `lines.flatMap(...)` and handles **each line on its own**. For each line it looks up the balance and computes `available` from that balance, unchanged. Line 1: is 30 more than 40? No, OK. Line 2: is 30 more than 40? It is the same balance of 40, so again no, OK. Nothing subtracts line 1's 30 before checking line 2. Both lines are approved and 60 units are reserved against 40: over-reserved by 20. The schema has no unique constraint on `(salesOrderId, skuId)`, so nothing stops an order from having two lines for one SKU.

Why the others are wrong:
- Lines are never merged; each is checked separately.
- There is no back-ordering logic; each line is approved or failed in full.
- The second line is checked against the same unchanged balance, so it is not rejected.

if (line.quantity > available) {

- **Duplicate SKU lines over-reserve.** `planReservation` checks each line separately (`inventoryRules.ts:30-57`), and `SalesOrderLine` has no unique constraint on `(salesOrderId, skuId)` (`prisma/schema.prisma:138-146`).

items.title: A double quote alone triggers quoting
items.body:
**Key: "Tote ""XL""", wrapped in quotes with each inner quote doubled.**

`csvCell` quotes a value when `text.includes(',') || text.includes('"')`. The name contains double quotes, so it takes the quoting branch: every `"` becomes `""`, and the result is wrapped in one pair of outer quotes. That is the standard CSV way to keep a quote inside a field.

Why the others are wrong:
- *unchanged*: a double quote is enough to trigger quoting; a comma is not required.
- *inner quotes left as is*: `replaceAll('"', '""')` doubles them.
- *no outer quotes*: the doubled text is always wrapped.

excerpts.quote: return text.includes(',') || text.includes('"') ? `"${text.replaceAll('"', '""')}"` : text

The matching Check does both. `?entityType=sales_order&entityId=so-10035` returns only that order's rows (the filter works), and `?limit=500` returns 400 with `error: "Invalid request"` (the validation rejects a limit over 100).
